eintraege.autor: European Union Institute for Security Studies (EUISS)
eintraege.kontext: In partnership between the European Union (EU) and the African Union (AU), The European Union Institute for Security Studies published a data-heavy report on EU-AU relations.
eintraege.gestaltung: A diagonal dot-based correlogram of leading causes of death, with categories arranged along a 45-degree axis and colored dots grouped by disease type, accompanied by a categorical legend.

eintraege.kontext: Does U.S. chocolate taste poorly compared to the same ones produced in Europe? Surbhi Bhatia uses data of each chocolate ingredients to find it out.
eintraege.gestaltung: A horizontal bar chart of minimum cocoa-solids requirements across countries, using Kit Kat bar images in place of conventional bars and an annotation noting the FAO 25% standard for milk chocolate.

eintraege.kontext: Checking who voted for what in Britain's election.
eintraege.gestaltung: Three side-by-side hexbin cartograms of the UK showing the 2015 results, 2017 results, and the change between them, with each constituency rendered as an equal-sized hexagon and a diverging Labour-to-Conservative scale for the shift in margin.

eintraege.titel: Years in office per government (Britain v Italy)
eintraege.kontext: A playful take on political (in)stability between Britain and Italy: each government is a triangle whose height is its time in office — Britain pointing up, Italy down. The punchline is that Giorgia Meloni has already outlasted three British prime ministers.
eintraege.gestaltung: An unusual mirror chart where each government is a right triangle growing with every year in office. I'm a bit skeptical — both axes encode time, and the area scales with the square of the duration, inflating long-lived governments. But it's original, readable and genuinely fun.

eintraege.titel: German Cheese Exports and Imports to/from Austria (2001–2025)
eintraege.kontext: Made for the #30DayChartChallenge (2026, day 21), this tracks Germany's cheese trade with Austria from 2001 to 2025. Both flows grew, but Germany long exported more than it imported — until the gap narrows and even flips in recent years. Data from Destatis.
eintraege.gestaltung: A trade-balance chart styled like an old engraved almanac: exports in gold, imports in dark ink, the gap between them shaded toward whoever leads. I love the antique typography and the curves labelled directly on the lines. A simple two-series chart given a strong editorial voice.

eintraege.titel: Sickness absence in the Netherlands is highest in health and social care
eintraege.kontext: Sickness absence across Dutch industries from 1996 to 2025, built by Datylon on CBS StatLine data. Health and social care has sat above the national average throughout, climbing after 2015 and spiking through the COVID years — and since 2018 it tops every Dutch industry.
eintraege.gestaltung: A line chart where every industry is a faint grey line, with just two pulled forward — Health and social care in orange, the overall mean in black — labelled at the line ends. A soft band flags the COVID window and four annotations anchored to key moments turn a tangle of trends into a guided story.

eintraege.titel: How much sleep do you really need? — beeswarm
eintraege.kontext: Part of a Reuters explainer on sleep, comparing how many hours a day different animals spend asleep — from the barely-sleeping red kangaroo to the marathon-napping armadillo, humans in the middle. Marine mammals sleep far less, many resting one brain hemisphere at a time so they can keep swimming.
eintraege.gestaltung: A beeswarm plot where each dot is a species along an axis of hours slept per day, split into a land row and a marine row. Filled dots are ordinary sleepers, hollow dots the unihemispheric ones — a neat way to encode a second qualitative variable without a colour legend. Direct labels and leader lines call out the outliers.

eintraege.titel: How much sleep do you really need? — sleep by age
eintraege.kontext: From the same Reuters piece, how much sleep we need at each stage of life, from newborns down to older adults. A dotted line separates total sleep across 24 hours, naps included, from sleep taken per night once daytime napping fades.
eintraege.gestaltung: A stacked bar chart with variable-width bars — each spans an age range, so width carries meaning as well as height. The recommended window is a hatched band bridging the asleep and awake zones, with sun and moon icons for the two halves of the day. Using the whole 24-hour clock as the frame turns a table of guidelines into a picture.

eintraege.kontext: Daily temperatures across France in 2026 versus the 1961–1990 normal, built by Dominic Royé from Open-Meteo (ERA5) data. Almost every day ran warmer than the baseline, with only a handful of brief cold spells — a whole year of climate deviation in one frame.
eintraege.gestaltung: A daily time series filled against the smooth 'normal' curve — red above, blue below — so the year reads as a wash of red. Two dashed curves mark the 5th–95th percentile envelope, and peaks above it read as record territory. The diverging fill against a reference line is a technique I love for anomaly data.

eintraege.titel: Share of world GDP over two centuries
eintraege.kontext: Two centuries of the world economy in one frame: each country's share of world GDP at purchasing-power parity from 1820 to 2025. It traces the rise and fall of great powers behind the article's theme of America's waning dominance. Made by Matt McLean for a piece by Sondre Ulvund Solstad in The Economist.
eintraege.gestaltung: A stacked area chart flipped on its side — time runs vertically, each country a coloured ribbon as wide as its GDP share. The ribbons reorder and weave past each other as ranks shift, giving a braided, woodgrain texture, with names dropped directly inside them. A gorgeous way to turn a dry stacked series into a two-century story.

eintraege.kontext: An animation of ERA5 reanalysis over Europe for June 2026, by Jeran Poehls, showing the 500 hPa wind field alongside 2-metre air temperature day by day. An anticyclone builds over western France in late June and drifts east — the signature of an early-summer heat build-up.
eintraege.gestaltung: A gorgeous scientific-art dataviz: wind is rendered as thousands of flowlines streaming across a 3D relief of Europe like windswept fur, coloured by temperature. The brushed-hair texture makes the atmosphere feel physical — not for reading exact values, but a mesmerising way to feel a month of weather.

eintraege.kontext: A data story by Toon Vos for The European Correspondent, from a manual count of 3,500 couches in IKEA catalogues from 1960 to 2021. European interiors grew steadily more muted and greyer through the 2010s — though, as ever, IKEA is now reviving bold designs from its archives.
eintraege.gestaltung: The chart itself is the argument — a row of vertical stripes, one per year, painted in that catalogue's two most prominent sofa colours, so six decades of taste read as a single colour gradient. Patterned years get a dotted checkerboard texture. I love letting the encoding literally be the subject: colour data shown as colour.

eintraege.kontext: A piece by Aliaksandra Shymanskaya and Liene Lūsīte, with visualisation by Sebastian Graeff, for The European Correspondent on how a warming climate is pushing ticks — some carrying Lyme disease or tick-borne encephalitis — further north, now even above the Arctic Circle.
eintraege.gestaltung: A gridded binned map: Europe is split into a square lattice, each cell shaded by how many tick species were recorded there. It's a 2D histogram over a map — like a hexbin map but with square bins — turning scattered points into a clean density surface. I like the restrained styling and the labelled dashed Arctic Circle line.

eintraege.titel: Water level of the Rhine in Cologne
eintraege.kontext: In August 2026 the Rhine at Cologne fell to a record low, well below the 2018 mark. Ansgar Wolsing charts the year's daily level against the historical envelope after a summer of drought and heat left Germany's main waterway too shallow for most loaded cargo ships — a stark image of the new climate reality.
eintraege.gestaltung: A time series where the 2026 daily level is a bold purple line over two nested grey bands: the full 2000–2025 range and, inside it, the 80% envelope. Watching the line dive out the bottom makes the anomaly legible. My favourite detail is the thin white stroke around the purple line that lifts it off the grey. Built in R.

eintraege.titel: Does AI stop children from learning?
eintraege.kontext: An Economist graphic from a June 2026 preprint of nearly 27,000 Chinese pupils. The finding: those using AI scored higher on homework and finished faster — but did worse at exam time. A cautionary tale about cognitive offloading; real learning still needs the hard work of grappling.
eintraege.gestaltung: Three stacked density panels — homework score, completion time, exam score — each comparing the same pupils before and while using AI, with a grey baseline for non-users. Read top to bottom, the 'using AI' hump slides right, then left, then left again. Showing the whole distribution rather than just means makes it quietly persuasive.

eintraege.titel: A day of trains across Europe
eintraege.kontext: An animated replay of one real day of scheduled trains across Germany, the Benelux, Switzerland and France, built from open GTFS timetables. A clock scrubs through the day while every service moves in its real position, colour-coded by category. It's one of sixteen rail networks the project covers.
eintraege.gestaltung: A dark-mode movement map where each train is a coloured dot trailing a comet tail, so the network pulses to life around hubs like Paris and Zürich. Rings bloom where a service begins, and speed and city presets let you explore. Rendered on plain HTML Canvas — no mapping library — a gorgeous flight-radar-style take on rail data.

eintraege.titel: Share of households with air conditioning
eintraege.kontext: Debates on air conditioning are raging in Europe this summer amid the heat waves. Our World in Data took a step back to compare AC usage across the world's main regions, revealing huge differences in adoption.
eintraege.gestaltung: A clean horizontal barplot ranking six regions by AC adoption, values at each bar end and two curly-brace annotations grouping the leaders and the laggards. A textbook case of how good labelling and a couple of annotations turn a plain bar chart into a finished story.

eintraege.titel: Hotel prices surge for the eclipse
eintraege.kontext: El País on how hotel prices exploded for Spain's 12 August 2026 total solar eclipse. Across the 23 provincial capitals in the path of totality, median Booking rates for eclipse night dwarfed a normal week — up to 879€ in Soria against 116€ seven days earlier.
eintraege.gestaltung: A dumbbell chart — a lollipop variant — joining each city's price a week before (blue) and on eclipse night (orange). It's the right pick for comparing two values across many groups: each bar's length is the price jump, instantly rankable.

eintraege.titel: The journey of a drop of water — France's watersheds
eintraege.kontext: We tend to assume a river flows to the nearest sea — but it often doesn't. Cartographer Perrin Remonté maps France's watersheds by where their water finally empties out, a quietly surprising way to redraw the country around its rivers rather than its borders.
eintraege.gestaltung: A hand-crafted cartographic poster colouring every drainage basin by its destination — blue for the Atlantic, Channel and North Sea, gold for the Mediterranean — over a delicate white river network. I really love the calm, appeasing palette and the elegant serif labelling of the seas and rivers.

eintraege.kontext: Alexander Bogachev turns every 2026 World Cup match into a 3D 'data portrait', each sculpted from around 1,500 match events. The goal isn't to report stats but to capture the emotional arc of a game — momentum swinging from one side to the other as the match is replayed on a timeline.
eintraege.gestaltung: Each half of the pitch rises into a coloured 3D terrain — one team blue, the other red — whose peaks trace where and how intensely the play surged, essentially a 2D density heatmap lifted into relief. A scrubber replays the match while a diverging momentum strip runs underneath. A gorgeous, genuinely fresh way to feel a familiar event.

eintraege.kontext: The summer of 2026 has been a brutal fire season in France — a moment that, for many, marked a real shift in how present and tangible the climate crisis suddenly felt. Le Monde tracks the cumulative area burned across the country against its full historical range since Effis records began in 2006.
eintraege.gestaltung: A cumulative area/line chart setting 2026 in deep red against the historical envelope — min, mean and max drawn as soft hatched stripes so the reference reads as context, not clutter. The red line tearing far above the max band, tagged with a single '×7.2', tells the whole story. I love the calm palette and the clean information hierarchy.

eintraege.kontext: As generative AI makes producing content nearly free, a natural worry follows: does more of it mean more of value, or just more? The Economist looks at monthly Amazon e-book releases, splitting them into AI-generated and non-AI titles to see how the flood has grown since ChatGPT arrived.
eintraege.gestaltung: A simple stacked area chart of monthly Amazon e-book releases: the AI-generated share in bold red stacked on the muted non-AI base, with an annotation marking ChatGPT-3.5's launch as the inflection point. The two categories are labelled directly on the areas, so no legend is needed. Simple yet devastatingly clear.

eintraege.kontext: Each country has a demographic fingerprint — how its people spread across ages, when they die, and when they have children. Benjamin Niedermann folds all three into one interactive profile, letting you sweep a country through ten-year snapshots from 1953 to 2023. Data from the UN's World Population Prospects 2024.
eintraege.gestaltung: A striking three-armed layout, each arm a distribution — a population pyramid, a mortality profile and a fertility curve — meeting over a map that anchors the chosen country. It's a bespoke, futuristic interactive UI; whether it adds much over a plain dropdown is fair to ask, but as design it's gorgeous. Made with VisQuill.

eintraege.titel: Strava as a proxy for where to live
eintraege.kontext: One of the most revealing 'unofficial' urban datasets isn't a property database — it's Strava. Its heatmaps show where people actually run and cycle, a rough proxy for where a city feels safe, green and pleasant. This one went viral off Matt's (@Terravoir) tweet: 'use Strava as a proxy for where to live'.
eintraege.gestaltung: Strava's global heatmap over Chicago, every street glowing brighter blue the more runners and cyclists trace it — an activity density heatmap laid over the road network. I love it when a dataviz jumps the fence and goes viral; a great reminder that a map can quietly shape real-life decisions like where to move.

eintraege.kontext: Coffee has become one of the most watched grocery items of the inflation era, but a single national average hides how differently the price moves from one city to the next. CostInflation tracks a seven-format basket — ground, beans, pods, instant, ready-to-drink, cold brew and creamer — and rebuilds the index daily.
eintraege.gestaltung: A line chart of the index with a shaded band showing the spread across cities, wrapped in the full dashboard toolkit: time frame buttons, date pickers, frequency and unit selectors, location filter and a tooltip. Nothing fancy, and that's the point — it's a solid reference for how to wire the classic controls around a time series.

eintraege.titel: The world's most liveable cities are among its least affordable
eintraege.kontext: Cities that top the quality-of-life rankings tend to be the ones you can least afford to move to. Home Economics puts Monocle's 2026 liveability list against Numbeo's home price-to-income ratios to show how much of that comfort is priced in.
eintraege.gestaltung: A beeswarm: every city is a circle placed along a log-scaled price-to-income axis, sized by average net salary, with the Monocle picks in blue against a grey crowd. Beautifully labelled with leader lines and a median reference. It's static though — I really wish I could search a city or hover a circle to reveal its name.

eintraege.kontext: Counting strikes tells you how bad a war is getting; counting the quiet days tells you something harder to look away from. Mariia Pushkarova takes Petro Ivaniuk's dataset of Russian missile and drone attacks on Ukraine and tracks, year by year, how many days passed with nothing at all — 266 in 2022, three so far in 2026.
eintraege.gestaltung: A calendar heatmap where every day is a dot, coloured by strike intensity, laid out as small multiples across five years with a donut summarising each one. I love it when a time series escapes the line chart: the opacity ramp makes the escalation almost physical, the grid filling up and darkening as you read left to right. Built in Tableau.

eintraege.autor: Adrien Dupas, Mélodie Lontjens & Philippine Robert (Le Point)
eintraege.kontext: Taxing the rich is a permanent fixture of French political debate, but "the rich" turns out to be half a dozen different populations: very high incomes, very high wealth, both at once, the top 0.1%, the top 0.001%. Le Point devoted a double page to untangling who actually pays what.
eintraege.gestaltung: The centrepiece: stacked areas splitting the effective tax rate by levy, walked along a logarithmic percentile axis so the top 0.0001% gets as much room as the merely rich — and you can watch the curve turn regressive. A dense, print-grade infographic where every panel uses a smart, unusual chart type. I love seeing numbers laid out like this.

eintraege.titel: 5% of US electricity is used for data centers
eintraege.kontext: Data centers are usually discussed as if they were about to swallow the grid, so the global figure tends to surprise people: it is small. Hannah Ritchie's point is that the average hides the concentration — behind Europe's number sits Ireland at over 20%, and behind the US number, Virginia at more than a quarter.
eintraege.gestaltung: A plain horizontal barplot, regions ranked, values sitting at the end of each bar and the United States picked out in dark red against a muted pink. The two-line note in the white space does the storytelling. I love that OWID charts are this simple yet efficient — you recognise their style instantly.

eintraege.titel: Reliance on Middle East oil and gas supplies
eintraege.kontext: Every flare-up in the Middle East raises the same question: who actually gets hurt if the barrels stop moving? The IEA measures each country's exposure as imports from the region over domestic demand plus exports, and compares 2017 with 2024 to show who has quietly grown more dependent.
eintraege.gestaltung: A circular barplot where each country is a radial bar for its reliance share, coloured by region, with a bubble on the outside sized by total import volume and a tick marking the earlier year. Clean, with just the right amount of interactivity to explore the data, and I really like the gradient on those outer bubbles.

eintraege.titel: Two centuries of French forest evolution
eintraege.kontext: Forests now cover a third of mainland France, roughly double what the 19th-century état-major maps recorded. But the regrowth is not a simple story: some old woodland vanished while new forest appeared elsewhere. This map from IGN's 2026 atlas compares the 1840-1866 and 2007-2018 forest cover in each département.
eintraege.gestaltung: A bubble map where each département gets two overlapping circles, forming a mini Venn diagram: surviving old forest, vanished old forest and recent forest. I'm not sure I like it: a map full of Venn diagrams is hard to read and the colors lack contrast. But it's a very innovative way to show a dataset I wouldn't know how to visualize otherwise.

eintraege.kontext: Global warming isn't just a shift of the average: extreme summers once considered near-impossible are becoming routine. Following Hansen, Sato & Ruedy (2012), this animation shows how far each place's summer sat from its 1951-1980 normal, year after year from 1941 to today.
eintraege.gestaltung: A density curve, colored by temperature class, that slides and flattens toward the hot side as the years go by, against the dashed 1951-1980 reference. Lovely to see temperatures kind of dancing. I'm not usually a fan of animation to show an evolution, but this one works quite well.

eintraege.titel: A warmer shape of summer, day by day
eintraege.kontext: August 2026 was hot in Europe. Using ERA5 data, Milos Popovic mapped the temperature anomaly for every single day of the month, compared to the 1991-2020 normal.
eintraege.gestaltung: An animated 3D map where both height and color encode the anomaly: warm regions rise, cool ones sink. Mesmerizing to see the planet breathing. I love the general layout, with the small barchart on the left giving the big picture of the month.

eintraege.titel: How Europe's intensifying marine heatwaves threaten its fisheries
eintraege.kontext: European seas just had their hottest summer on record, and the heat is transforming the marine ecosystems coastal communities rely on. This Reuters scrollytelling piece by Ben Welsh and colleagues follows the numbers from the data out to Spanish and English fishermen.
eintraege.gestaltung: The article opens on an animated 3D map built with deck.gl, where each sea grid cell becomes a bar whose height and color show the daily temperature anomaly. A bold choice for gridded climate data, and it works: the orange spikes rising over the Mediterranean are striking.

eintraege.kontext: Which of the world's most forested countries gained or lost trees since 2000? This chart, shared on r/dataisbeautiful, compares the net forest-area change of the 10 countries with the largest forests in 2000, using FAO data.
eintraege.gestaltung: A diverging barplot built with Matplotlib, with bars going left or right from zero. Mirror barplots are perfect to show values diverging from 0, and the double encoding (direction + green/brown color) makes the change obvious. The extra column with the relative change is a nice touch.

eintraege.titel: How long do you really wait for your bus in Singapore?
eintraege.kontext: Every commuter knows the frustration of a bus that doesn't show up on time. This Straits Times scrollytelling piece opens with the questions riders ask themselves, then digs into the frequency and reliability of each Singapore bus service.
eintraege.gestaltung: A circular line chart: the dashed circle is the scheduled arrival, and each red line wobbles outward with every delay. I love the minimalist style, and how the chart almost becomes an illustration embedded in the article. A dropdown lets you find your own bus.

eintraege.kontext: France gained 28 million people since 1876, yet six communes out of ten are less populated today than back then. This animation replays every census since 1876 to show how the population drained from the countryside to cities and coasts.
eintraege.gestaltung: An animated population density map, rendered like a glowing contour relief. I usually don't like animation to show a time series, but here it really works: you see the population shrink into the cities. Another chart type would not convey this story as strongly.

eintraege.titel: Child mortality has declined in all world regions
eintraege.kontext: In 1950, almost one in four children worldwide died before their fifth birthday. Max Roser shows how this rate has fallen in every world region since, while reminding us that progress is far from finished.
eintraege.gestaltung: A line chart with no Y axis: only the first and last data points are labelled, which is smart since that's where the exact values matter. Lines are also directly labelled, so no legend is needed.

eintraege.kontext: When was the building you live in actually built? Alexander Bogachev maps all 122,435 buildings of Paris in 3D, colored by construction period, from the medieval core to recent towers, so you can watch the city grow and explore any street.
eintraege.gestaltung: The opening animation is stunning. I love the histogram at the bottom, where each dot stacks buildings by year: always a great combo with a map, and it doubles as a timeline slider to filter by period.

eintraege.titel: Road accident density along Norway's roads
eintraege.kontext: Where do crashes actually happen along a road? Inspired by a Visquill chart of the UK's A1, Thomas Heggelund maps 25 years of car accidents along any Norwegian highway using official NVDB data from Statens vegvesen.
eintraege.gestaltung: A histogram wrapped along the road itself: each bar sticks out sideways from its stretch of road, with length and color showing accident count, so hotspots like Bergen jump out. Bin size, year range and a circular time-of-day picker let you dig in.

eintraege.titel: The dark novel of French debt
eintraege.kontext: France's public debt has passed 3,000 billion euros. In a cover story titled Le roman noir de la dette française, Le Point retraces 50 years of uncontrolled drift, from Giscard d'Estaing to Macron. Infographic by Clara Dealberto.
eintraege.gestaltung: A single line chart, but packed with annotations: every key event (oil shock, Maastricht, subprime crisis, Covid…) is pinned to its point, and shaded bands mark each presidency. I love how so much annotation tells most of the story with one simple line.

eintraege.kontext: For Pacific island nations, climate change is not an abstraction. A Fiji-based data analyst explores how the region is living it through a scrollytelling piece, here showing how rainfall has become unpredictable and irregular across 22 countries and territories.
eintraege.gestaltung: A ridgeline of rainfall anomalies where each country's curve swings above or below its baseline, with a soft blue gradient fill. A mesmerizing article with just the right amount of animation and some original chart types in use.

eintraege.kontext: Will AI be good or bad for humanity? A GlobeScan survey asked people in 13 countries, and the answer depends a lot on where you live: emerging economies are enthusiastic while rich Western countries are far more wary. France, unsurprisingly, is the most reluctant of all.
eintraege.gestaltung: A horizontal stacked barplot with a diverging blue-to-red palette, from very positive to very negative. Subtle but smart: countries seem ranked by the share of no impact + negative answers rather than by positive ones, which makes the pessimistic block grow steadily down the chart.

eintraege.kontext: Most midterm coverage compared the 2026 House vote to 2024 with simple straight arrows. The New York Times added 2020 to the picture, revealing that many demographic groups did not just swing back to the Democrats: they returned to, or went past, where they stood four years earlier.
eintraege.gestaltung: A brilliant twist on the dumbbell chart: each group gets a U-turn shaped arrow going from 2020 to 2024 and then to 2026, colored by direction. I had never seen anything like it before, a fully original way to show two successive shifts in a single mark.

eintraege.kontext: How warm is the planet today compared to the past? Copernicus updates its Climate Pulse dashboard every day with near-real-time global temperatures, letting anyone put the latest data in the perspective of every year since 1940.
eintraege.gestaltung: A line chart highlighting one year against all the others in grey, next to a globe of temperature anomalies. Beautiful design with just the right amount of info displayed by default, and a lot more hidden under buttons for those who want to dig in.
